concepts.gloss: A five-valued formal system categorising clauses as declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative, or imperative.

concepts.term: characteristic use of a clause type
concepts.gloss: The typical illocutionary use linked to a syntactic clause type without requiring that use in every instance.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: The characteristic use of an exclamative clause, distinguished from exclamatory delivery of other clause types.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: A type of illocutionary force encompassing requests, instructions, commands and similar attempts to influence behaviour.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: A particular clause instance belongs to one major clause type, even when the same abstract string admits more than one analysis.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: A string whose punctuation, context or intonation allows different analyses as clause types, resolved in an individual instance.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: A coordinated sentence in which individual clauses have distinct grammatical clause types.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: A clause lacking a verb that can nevertheless bear a clause-type classification, such as an open interrogative or exclamative.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: A repetition or clarification request built on an earlier utterance, superimposed on rather than replacing the utterance's clause type.

sources.section: §1 Type as a grammatical system of the clause

concepts.gloss: The application of declarative, closed/open interrogative, or exclamative categories to subordinate clauses.

rules.concept: clause type applies to clauses rather than whole sentences
rules.statement: Clause type categorises each clause, including subordinate clauses, rather than the whole sentence; coordinated clauses may have different types within one sentence.
rules.condition: When assigning a clause-type category, classify each clause independently, particularly in a sentence that coordinates clauses of different types, instead of assigning a single clause type to their entire coordination.

The train is early, but get ready to leave. [declarative + imperative]
How remarkable the result is, and it came so quickly! [exclamative + declarative]

rules.concept: mutually exclusive clause types and ambiguity
rules.statement: The five grammatical clause types are mutually exclusive for any individual clause instance, although an abstract string without prosodic or contextual specification can permit more than one clause-type analysis.
rules.condition: For a particular spoken or written clause in context, assign one of declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative or imperative; when a string is ambiguous without punctuation, intonation or context, record competing possible analyses rather than two simultaneous type memberships.

contrast.text: How many visitors returned? [open interrogative reading]
How many visitors returned! [exclamative reading of the same words]
You have finished the assignment. [declarative instance]
Have you finished the assignment? [closed interrogative instance]

rules.concept: echo question as a cross-cutting construction
rules.statement: An echo question requests repetition or clarification of a previous utterance and is not a sixth grammatical clause type: the echo feature can occur with multiple major clause types.
rules.condition: Where a speaker repeats part of a preceding clause while querying an item, classify the echoed clause's grammatical type independently of its echo-question use; an echo based on an imperative remains imperative, and an echo based on a closed interrogative remains closed interrogative.

contrast.text: Pass the folder to Maren. [imperative stimulus]
Pass the folder to whom? [imperative echo question]
Did you order a projector? [closed interrogative stimulus]
Did I order a what? [closed interrogative echo question]

rules.concept: verbless clause fragments retain clause type
rules.statement: Certain verbless clause fragments can be classified as open interrogatives or exclamatives even though they lack a finite verb.
rules.condition: When identifying an utterance such as what about X or an exclamative what + NP fragment, classify its clause type by the relevant construction rather than requiring a finite verbal clause.
